grade_rationale.text: Every verified peoples_regions row is Russians: Afanasyev calls Gorynych the Russian name of the mythic serpent, and Ralston places Zmei Goruinuich in Russian story-land and Russian fable.

Ralston's two books are one source, and his Songs of the Russian People leans on Afanasyev on the Gorynych pages (a footnote to 'Afanasief, P. V. S. II.' in the Zmyei paragraph, and 'says Afanasief' in the Buyan passage), so Ralston is not counted as fully independent of Afanasyev.

Afanasyev quotes the folk texts themselves rather than only interpreting: bylina lines of Dobrynya and Gorynchishche, and a song of the princess and the serpent Gorynich, citing Kirsha Danilov, Kireevsky's songs and a song printed in the Academy's Izvestiya supplement.
Afanasyev also cites a separate Siberian tale of Zmey Gorynych in the Urals from the Finsky Vestnik of 1845, and folk tales (skazki) of the princess and the charmer Zmey Gorynych.
Ralston's Russian Folk-Tales names Zmei Goruinuich as the many-headed Snake of Russian story-land without attributing the statement to Afanasyev on that page.
